query_text: first satellite compared to the latest

messages.content: first satellite compared to the latest

message.content:
The **first artificial satellite** was **Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957.[2][3] If by “the latest” you mean the most recent satellite in general, there is no single global “latest satellite” because new satellites are launched continuously by many countries and companies.

A useful comparison is that **Sputnik 1** was a **small, simple, non-scientific beacon satellite**: about **58 cm** in diameter, **83.6 kg**, with a radio transmitter and batteries, and it orbited Earth in about **98 minutes**.[2] By contrast, modern satellites are typically far more specialized and capable, with scientific instruments, navigation payloads, communications systems, Earth-imaging sensors, or deep-space hardware; the development from Sputnik to later missions like **Explorer I** showed this shift toward satellites carrying useful scientific payloads.[2][5]

If you meant **“latest satellite” as the newest major milestone**, one strong example from the sources is **Explorer I**, launched by the United States on January 31, 1958; it was still lighter than Sputnik but carried a scientific payload that discovered Earth’s radiation belts.[2][5]

If you want, I can also give you a **side-by-side comparison table** of **Sputnik 1 vs. a modern satellite**.
